citation.title: Combining List Experiment and Direct Question Estimates of Sensitive Behavior Prevalence
citation.venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 46 (PDF p. 4)] Suppose we have a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population. Let $X_i = 1$ if subject $i$ engages in a sensitive behavior and $X_i = 0$ otherwise. We attempt to measure the behavior $X_i$ using two methods: direct questioning and list experimentation. Our goal is to identify the prevalence of the sensitive behavior in the population, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$. Let $Y_i$ be the report of subject $i$ to the direct question. We assume that, under direct questioning, subjects may lie and claim that they do not engage in the behavior but will not lie and falsely claim that they do engage in the behavior. [Assumption 1: p. 46] Assumption 1 (Monotonicity). There exist three latent classes of respondents under direct questioning: those who do not engage in the behavior and report truthfully ($X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 0$), subjects who engage and report truthfully ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$), and subjects who engage but report that they do not, i.e., withhold ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 0$). [Direct response: p. 46] Let $p = \Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid X_i = 1]$ be the probability of a subject reporting truthfully to the direct question, given that he or she engages in the sensitive behavior. The response of subject $i$ is $Y_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - \mu + \mu(1 - p) \\ 1 & \text{with probability } \mu p. \end{cases}$ [p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] The probability that subject $i$ engages in the behavior, given a negative response, is therefore $\Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$. While direct questioning is sufficient to reveal $\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \mu p$, it is not sufficient to identify $\Pr[Y_i = 0 \mid X_i = 1] = 1 - p$. [List experiment: p. 47] Suppose we have a treatment $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. In the list experiment, treated subjects ($Z_i = 1$) receive a number of control questions and an additional question about the sensitive behavior. We denote the number of items that the subject states are applicable with $V_i$. [Assumption 2: p. 47] Assumption 2 (No Liars and No Design Effects). Reframing Imai’s (2011) formulations, we observe $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$, where $W_i$ is the baseline outcome (under control) for subject $i$ for the list experiment. [Assumption 3: p. 47] We further require that the treatment assignment be independent of the actual behavior, direct question, and baseline response. This is a stricter variant of Imai’s (2011) ignorability assumption. Assumption 3 (Treatment Independence). $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$. [Assumption 4: p. 47] To ensure that all target quantities are well defined (and, later, to facilitate inference), we impose the mild regularity condition that all population variances are positive. Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions). $\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = y] > 0$, for $z, y \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{Var}[Z_i] > 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Y_i] > 0$. [Estimators: Section 3, p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] Define the sample means: $\bar Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i$, $\bar V_{1,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i (1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i (1 - Y_i)}$ and $\bar V_{0,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}$. Define an estimator of $\mu$ based on (1), $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$. Let $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ be the probability of receiving the treatment question in the list experiment. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)}$. [Not printed as assumptions, but used throughout] The paper states the sampling model only as 'a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population'; its proofs treat $(W_i, X_i, Y_i, Z_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, as independent and identically distributed, with $Z_i$ part of the draw and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \gamma$ (in the application, p. 53 (PDF p. 11): 'All randomizations used Bernoulli random assignment with equal probability 0.5'). $V_i$ is a count of items on a fixed finite list and is therefore bounded; no moment condition is printed. Assumption 1 is used in the form $Y_i \le X_i$ (no subject has $X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$). The subgroup means are ratios, and the paper assigns them no value when a $(Z, Y)$ cell of the sample is empty (P019-E003). Printed page numbers are PDF page numbers plus 42. Appendices C to F are in the online supplement (author-appendix.pdf, 7 pp.), not in the article PDF.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1 (Placebo Test I), the sentence on tests of distributional equality, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement; $V_i - 1$ replaces the printed $V_i + 1$, which is Sol's smallest repair; everything else is as printed] It is possible to jointly test the Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence assumptions. Under these assumptions, for all $t$, $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i = (t + 1) \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$, thus tests of distributional equality are appropriate. Any valid test of distributional equality between $V_i$ (under $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$) and $V_i - 1$ (under $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$) will permit rejection of the null. [Hypotheses of the formal content, in full] $Y_i \le X_i$ (Assumption 1); $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$ (Assumption 2); $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$ (Assumption 3); and $\Pr[Z_i = z, Y_i = 1] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, so that the conditional distributions are defined (implied by Assumption 4). [Conclusion] The conditional distribution of $V_i$ given $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$ equals the conditional distribution of $V_i - 1$ given $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$: for all $t$, $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i - 1 = t \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$; both equal $\Pr[W_i = t \mid Y_i = 1]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, $W_i$, $V_i$ and Assumptions 1–4 as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–47, PDF pp. 4–5). The 'null' of the sentence is the joint hypothesis that Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects and Treatment Independence hold.
canonical_claim.note: Equivalently one may compare $V_i + 1$ under $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$ with $V_i$ under $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$ (the earlier round's correction lists both forms). Derivation (the artifact, section 'E001 and N001'): among $Y_i = 1$, Assumption 1 gives $X_i = 1$; Assumption 2 gives $V_i = W_i$ under control and $V_i = W_i + 1$ under treatment; Assumption 3 gives the same conditional law of $W_i$ given $Y_i = 1$ in the two arms. Taking means gives $\beta = 1$ (P019-T12). The clause about what a valid test 'will permit' is not formal; the formal content is the equality of the two conditional distributions under the null.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix C, first paragraph, the sentence 'If this estimate is different from 1.0, it must either be because ...', as printed
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 2, Appendix C, first paragraph, third sentence. Not in main.pdf; the main-text counterpart is Section 4.1 and Proposition 3, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Supplement p. 2, Appendix C, first paragraph] The placebo test proposed in Section 4 is a joint test of Assumptions 1-3 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence). In brief, the test considers whether the conventional list experimental estimate appears to be significantly different from 1.0 among the subset of subjects who answer “Yes” to the direct question. If this estimate is different from 1.0, it must either be because a) some of those who answer “Yes” are falsely confessing (thereby violating monotonicity) or b) the standard list experiment assumptions of No Liars and No Design Effects are not met. [Counterexample, from the validator: the population contrast differs from 1 with no false confession, no liar and no design effect] Let $B, C, X, Z$ be independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$) variables (sixteen atoms of probability $\frac{1}{16}$) and set $W = B + C$, $Y = X\,\mathbf{1}\{C = Z\}$ and $V = W + XZ$. Then: (a) $Y \le X$, so nobody falsely confesses and Assumption 1 holds, with $\Pr[X = 0, Y = 0] = \frac{1}{2}$, $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 0] = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 1] = \frac{1}{4}$; (b) $V = W + XZ$, with $W \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ not depending on $Z$, so Assumption 2 (No Liars and No Design Effects) holds; (c) Assumption 4 holds: the cells $(Z, Y) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ have probabilities $\frac{3}{8}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{3}{8}, \frac{1}{8}$, conditional means of $V$ equal to $\frac{7}{6}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{7}{6}, \frac{5}{2}$ and conditional variances of $V$ equal to $\frac{17}{36}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{17}{36}, \frac{1}{4}$, with $\mathrm{Var}[Y] = \frac{3}{16}$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Z] = \frac{1}{4}$; (d) $Z$ is independent of $(B, C, X)$, hence of $(W, X)$ and of the potential answers $Y(0) = X(1 - C)$ and $Y(1) = XC$, and $Y$ is independent of $Z$, with $\delta = E[Y \mid Z = 1] - E[Y \mid Z = 0] = 0$; (e) Assumption 3 fails: $\Pr[(W, X, Y) = (0, 1, 0), Z = 0] = 0$ while $\Pr[(W, X, Y) = (0, 1, 0)]\Pr[Z = 0] = \frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{32}$; (f) $\beta = E[V \mid Z = 1, Y = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0, Y = 1] = \frac{5}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 2 \ne 1$. So the list difference in means among those who answer “Yes” differs from 1 although neither a) nor b) of the printed sentence holds; only Treatment Independence fails. [A second instance, the candidate's] With $B, C, Z$ independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$), $X = 1$, $W = B + C$, $Y = \mathbf{1}\{C = Z\}$ and $V = W + Z$ (eight atoms of probability $\frac{1}{8}$): Assumptions 1, 2 and 4 hold (every $(Z, Y)$ cell has probability $\frac{1}{4}$ and conditional variance $\frac{1}{4}$), Assumption 3 fails, $\delta = 0$ and $\beta = \frac{5}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [Placebo Test II: Section 4.2, p. 51 (PDF p. 9)] Define $\delta = E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]$. [Assumption 3 and what violates it: p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; 'Assumption 3 would be violated if (i) we did not have random assignment of the treatment or (ii) there are additional design effects; e.g., the treatment assignment affects the response to the direct question.' 'No Design Effects' in the printed sentence has the meaning of Assumption 2: the baseline list response $W_i$ does not change when the sensitive item is added. 'This estimate' is read as the population contrast $\beta$ (a sample estimate can differ from 1 by sampling variation under every assumption).
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor: the two listed causes are presented as exhaustive, and they are not. The validator's check.py enumerates both instances with exact rational arithmetic (exact-output.txt beside the derivation), including the full test of joint independence over every support cell; a second validator upheld it. In both instances the treatment is randomized independently of all latent types and potential responses, but the observed direct answer depends on the assignment, so the “Yes” respondents in the two arms differ in baseline composition: $E[W \mid Z = 1, Y = 1] = \frac{3}{2}$ and $E[W \mid Z = 0, Y = 1] = \frac{1}{2}$. Both instances have $\delta = 0$, so Placebo Test II's population null holds; Proposition 4 states a necessary consequence of Assumption 3, not a sufficient condition. The unconditional list contrast is unaffected: $E[V \mid Z = 1] - E[V \mid Z = 0] = E[X]$, which is $\frac{1}{2}$ in the first instance and 1 in the second. The counterexample does not touch Proposition 3, whose hypotheses include Treatment Independence, nor the supplement's simulations, in which direct answers are fixed before assignment.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Appendix C, first paragraph, the sentence 'If this estimate is different from 1.0, it must either be because ...', corrected
canonical_claim.location: Online supplement (author-appendix.pdf) p. 2, Appendix C, first paragraph, third sentence
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement; Sol's smallest repair, which adds failure of Assumption 3 as a third possible cause] If the population difference-in-means among subjects who answer “Yes” is different from 1.0, at least one of Assumptions 1-3 must fail: some subjects falsely confess, No Liars or No Design Effects fails, or Treatment Independence fails. A statistically significant sample departure is evidence against this joint null. [Formal content, with every hypothesis] Suppose $\Pr[Z_i = z, Y_i = 1] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, so that $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$ is defined. (i) If $Y_i \le X_i$ (Assumption 1) and $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$ (Assumption 2), then $\beta = 1 + E[W_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[W_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. (ii) If in addition $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$ (Assumption 3), then $E[W_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] = E[W_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$ and $\beta = 1$. (iii) Hence if $\beta \ne 1$, at least one of Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 fails; and if Assumptions 1 and 2 hold and $\beta \ne 1$, then Assumption 3 fails.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). Assumptions 1–4 as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–47, PDF pp. 4–5).
canonical_claim.note: The repair weakens the diagnostic conclusion only: a failed Placebo Test I cannot in general be attributed to false confessions or to list-response violations. It adds no assumption and changes no estimand or test. The validator records an alternative, to prefix the original sentence with 'Provided Assumption 3 (Treatment Independence) holds', which is correct but restricts its scope; this target follows the third-alternative repair. Parts (i) and (ii) are equation (1) of the artifact and the step after it; (ii) is the first sentence of Proposition 3 with its assumption range corrected (P019-T12), and (iii) is its contrapositive. The last sentence of the repair, about a statistically significant sample departure, is not formal.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.3, 'a joint test via Fisher’s method is insignificant as well' (the chi-square reference distribution of the joint test of the five Study B placebo tests), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 56 (PDF p. 14), Section 5.3, paragraph on Table 7; Table 7 is on p. 57 (PDF p. 15)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 56 (PDF p. 14), Section 5.3] The results of Placebo Test I for Study B are presented in table 7. Among the subgroup of respondents who answer “Yes” to the direct question, the list experiment difference-in-means estimate $\beta$ should be equal to 1, under Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence). None of the values of $\beta$ are statistically significantly different from 1 using the placebo test, and a joint test via Fisher’s method is insignificant as well. [What is refuted] The printed sentence gives no premise for the joint test beyond the per-list Assumptions 1–4. The counterexample shows that those assumptions, holding for every list together with independent Bernoulli assignments, do not imply that Fisher's statistic $T = -2\sum_{j=1}^{5}\log p_j$ has the $\chi^2_{10}$ reference distribution in the limit. [Counterexample, from the validator; it respects the order of Study B, lists before direct questions] For each respondent draw seven independent fair bits: $D \in \{0, 1\}$, a sign $U \in \{-1, 1\}$ and $Z_1, \ldots, Z_5 \in \{0, 1\}$ (128 atoms of probability $\frac{1}{128}$). Let $A_j = 2Z_j - 1$, $P_j = \prod_{k=1}^{j} A_k$ with $P_0 = 1$, and $F_j = \prod_{k=j+1}^{5} A_k$ with $F_5 = 1$. For $j = 1, \ldots, 5$ set $X_j = D$, $W_j = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{2}U P_{j-1}$, $Y_j = D\,\mathbf{1}\{F_j = 1\}$ and $V_j = W_j + D Z_j$. Then for every list $j$: (a) $Y_j \le X_j$ (Assumption 1); (b) $V_j = W_j + X_j Z_j$ with $W_j \in \{1, 2\}$ (Assumption 2); (c) $(W_j, X_j, Y_j)$ is a function of $D$, $U$ and the assignments other than $Z_j$, and is independent of $Z_j$ (Assumption 3); (d) $\Pr[Y_j = 1] = \frac{1}{4}$ for $j < 5$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ for $j = 5$, $\mathrm{Var}[Z_j] = \frac{1}{4}$, and $\mathrm{Var}[V_j \mid Z_j = z, Y_j = y]$ equals $\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{17}{36}, \frac{1}{4}$ for $(z, y) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ when $j < 5$ and $\frac{1}{4}$ in all four cells when $j = 5$ (Assumption 4); (e) $Z_1, \ldots, Z_5$ are independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$); (f) $E[W_j \mid Y_j = 1] = \frac{3}{2}$ and $\beta_j = 1$. The influence functions are $\psi_j = 2DU(P_j + P_5)$ for $j < 5$ and $\psi_5 = 2DUP_5$, so $E[\psi_j] = 0$ and $E[\psi\psi^{\top}]$ has diagonal $(4, 4, 4, 4, 2)$ and every off-diagonal entry equal to 2. The five standardized placebo statistics therefore converge jointly to $G_j = (E_j + E_5)/\sqrt{2}$ for $j < 5$ and $G_5 = E_5$, with $E_1, \ldots, E_5$ independent standard normal: each is standard normal, with correlation $\frac{1}{2}$ among the first four and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ between each of them and the fifth. Each $p$-value is asymptotically uniform, and $T$ converges in distribution to $\sum_{j=1}^{5} g(G_j)$ with $g(x) = -2\log(2\Phi(-|x|))$, whose variance is $20 + 12\,\mathrm{Var}(h(E_5)) + 8\,\mathrm{Cov}(h(E_5), g(E_5)) > 20$, where $h(t) = E[g((E + t)/\sqrt{2})]$ for $E$ standard normal. A $\chi^2_{10}$ variable has variance 20, so the limit distribution of $T$ is not $\chi^2_{10}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Fisher's method; not defined in the paper] With $p_1, \ldots, p_5$ the five Placebo Test I $p$-values of Table 7 (p. 57, PDF p. 15: 0.294, 0.339, 0.309, 0.293, 0.256), the statistic is $T = -2\sum_{j=1}^{5}\log p_j$, referred to the $\chi^2$ distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, which is the distribution of $T$ when the five $p$-values are independent and uniform on $(0, 1)$. [Per-list quantities] For list $j = 1, \ldots, 5$ the paper's objects carry a subscript $j$: $X_j$, $Y_j$, $Z_j$, $W_j$, $V_j = W_j + X_j Z_j$, $\beta_j = E[V_j \mid Z_j = 1, Y_j = 1] - E[V_j \mid Z_j = 0, Y_j = 1]$, with $\hat\beta_j$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]$ as in Section 4.1 (p. 50, PDF p. 8) and $p_j = 2\Phi\left(-|\hat\beta_j - 1| / \sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]}\right)$ (Proposition 3). The paper states Assumptions 1–4 for a single list; in the application each respondent answers five lists and five direct questions, with each list treatment assigned independently with probability 0.5 (p. 53, PDF p. 11), and in Study B the lists come before the direct questions. [Influence function, from the validator] $q_j = \Pr[Y_j = 1]$, $\gamma_j = \Pr[Z_j = 1]$, $m_j = E[W_j \mid Y_j = 1]$ and $\psi_j = \frac{Y_j Z_j}{q_j\gamma_j}(V_j - m_j - 1) - \frac{Y_j(1 - Z_j)}{q_j(1 - \gamma_j)}(V_j - m_j)$, for which $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_j - 1) = n^{-1/2}\sum_i \psi_{ij} + o_p(1)$ under Assumptions 1–4 for list $j$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact, over the 128 atoms (verified by the validator's check_exact.py with rational arithmetic, model 'sequential_spillovers'): items (a) to (f); the pointwise identity $\psi_j = \frac{Y_j}{q_j}\cdot\frac{Z_j - \gamma_j}{\gamma_j(1 - \gamma_j)}\,(W_j - m_j)$, which here is $2DU(P_j + P_5)$ for $j < 5$ and $2DUP_5$ for $j = 5$; $E[\psi_j] = 0$; and the matrix $E[\psi\psi^{\top}]$ with rows $(4,2,2,2,2)$, $(2,4,2,2,2)$, $(2,2,4,2,2)$, $(2,2,2,4,2)$, $(2,2,2,2,2)$. Exact, about the normal law: for $G$ standard normal, $g(G) = -2\log(2\Phi(-|G|))$ has the $\chi^2_2$ distribution (mean 2, variance 4), because $2\Phi(-|G|)$ is uniform on $(0, 1)$; conditional on $E_5$ the variables $g(G_1), \ldots, g(G_4)$ are independent with mean $h(E_5)$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(g(G_j), g(G_k)) = \mathrm{Var}(h(E_5))$ for $j \ne k < 5$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(g(G_j), g(G_5)) = \mathrm{Cov}(h(E_5), g(E_5))$; $h$ and $g$ are even and strictly increasing in the absolute value of the argument, which gives $\mathrm{Var}(h(E_5)) > 0$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(h(E_5), g(E_5)) > 0$; hence $\mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_j g(G_j)\right) = 5 \cdot 4 + 12\,\mathrm{Var}(h(E_5)) + 8\,\mathrm{Cov}(h(E_5), g(E_5)) > 20$. Asymptotic: the passage from the sample statistics to the limit (the multivariate central limit theorem for the $\psi$ and consistency of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]$).
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor: an unstated premise, with the reported arithmetic and the non-rejection correct (Fisher statistic 12.143, $p = 0.276$; a covariance-aware joint Wald test gives 5.147 on 5 degrees of freedom, $p = 0.398$). The counterexample is an artificial null model, not a description of the survey; it establishes the missing implication, not dependence in the data, and inequality (7) of the artifact does not by itself give a size distortion at the 0.05 cutoff. The artifact (section 4) also has a simpler instance with a closed-form limit, which does not respect the list-before-direct order: with the same bits, $X_j = Y_j = D$, $W_j = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\prod_{k \ne j} A_k$ and $V_j = W_j + D Z_j$, every per-list assumption holds, $\beta_j = 1$, $\psi_j = 2D\prod_{k=1}^{5} A_k$ for every $j$, $E[\psi\psi^{\top}]$ has every entry equal to 2, the five limiting $p$-values coincide with one uniform variable $Q$, and $T$ converges to $-10\log Q$, with $\Pr(T \ge t) = e^{-t/10}$, mean 10 and variance 100. A third model ('stable') has all outcomes shared across lists and $E[\psi\psi^{\top}] = 2I_5$: shared respondents alone do not break the reference distribution. A second validator re-ran the exact check and upheld it.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.3, the joint test via Fisher’s method, corrected (with the premise it needs)
canonical_claim.location: p. 56 (PDF p. 14), Section 5.3, paragraph on Table 7
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement; Sol's smallest repair, which states the additional joint premise] Assuming asymptotic independence of the five placebo statistics, Fisher’s method gives a joint statistic of 12.143 on 10 degrees of freedom ($p = 0.276$), and does not reject the common null. [A sufficient premise and the formal content, from the validator's derivation, sections 1 and 2] [Hypotheses] Respondents are independent and identically distributed. For each list $j = 1, \ldots, 5$, Assumptions 1–4 hold: $Y_j \le X_j$; $V_j = W_j + X_j Z_j$; $(W_j, X_j, Y_j) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_j$; and the non-degeneracy conditions of Assumption 4. In addition, the assignments $Z_1, \ldots, Z_5$ are mutually independent, and the whole assignment vector $(Z_1, \ldots, Z_5)$ is independent of $L = (W_1, \ldots, W_5, X_1, \ldots, X_5, Y_1, \ldots, Y_5)$. The list responses are bounded. [Conclusion] (i) $\beta_j = 1$ for every $j$. (ii) With $\psi_j = \frac{Y_j}{q_j}\cdot\frac{Z_j - \gamma_j}{\gamma_j(1 - \gamma_j)}\,(W_j - m_j)$, $E[\psi_j \psi_k \mid L] = 0$ and hence $E[\psi_j\psi_k] = 0$ for $j \ne k$: the limiting covariance matrix of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_1 - 1, \ldots, \hat\beta_5 - 1)$ is diagonal. (iii) The five statistics $(\hat\beta_j - 1)/\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]}$ converge jointly in distribution to five independent standard normal variables; the five two-sided $p$-values $p_j = 2\Phi\left(-|\hat\beta_j - 1|/\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]}\right)$ converge jointly to independent uniform variables on $(0, 1)$; and $T = -2\sum_{j=1}^{5}\log p_j$ converges in distribution to $\chi^2_{10}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Fisher's method; not defined in the paper] With $p_1, \ldots, p_5$ the five Placebo Test I $p$-values of Table 7 (p. 57, PDF p. 15: 0.294, 0.339, 0.309, 0.293, 0.256), the statistic is $T = -2\sum_{j=1}^{5}\log p_j$, referred to the $\chi^2$ distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, which is the distribution of $T$ when the five $p$-values are independent and uniform on $(0, 1)$. [Per-list quantities] For list $j = 1, \ldots, 5$ the paper's objects carry a subscript $j$: $X_j$, $Y_j$, $Z_j$, $W_j$, $V_j = W_j + X_j Z_j$, $\beta_j = E[V_j \mid Z_j = 1, Y_j = 1] - E[V_j \mid Z_j = 0, Y_j = 1]$, with $\hat\beta_j$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]$ as in Section 4.1 (p. 50, PDF p. 8) and $p_j = 2\Phi\left(-|\hat\beta_j - 1| / \sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta_j]}\right)$ (Proposition 3). The paper states Assumptions 1–4 for a single list; in the application each respondent answers five lists and five direct questions, with each list treatment assigned independently with probability 0.5 (p. 53, PDF p. 11), and in Study B the lists come before the direct questions. [Influence function, from the validator] $q_j = \Pr[Y_j = 1]$, $\gamma_j = \Pr[Z_j = 1]$, $m_j = E[W_j \mid Y_j = 1]$ and $\psi_j = \frac{Y_j Z_j}{q_j\gamma_j}(V_j - m_j - 1) - \frac{Y_j(1 - Z_j)}{q_j(1 - \gamma_j)}(V_j - m_j)$, for which $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_j - 1) = n^{-1/2}\sum_i \psi_{ij} + o_p(1)$ under Assumptions 1–4 for list $j$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) Under Assumptions 1–3 for list $j$ and $\Pr[Z_j = z, Y_j = 1] > 0$: $\beta_j = 1$ (P019-T12). (b) Pointwise, using $V_j = W_j + Z_j$ when $Y_j = 1$: $\frac{Y_j Z_j}{q_j\gamma_j}(V_j - m_j - 1) - \frac{Y_j(1 - Z_j)}{q_j(1 - \gamma_j)}(V_j - m_j) = \frac{Y_j}{q_j}\cdot\frac{Z_j - \gamma_j}{\gamma_j(1 - \gamma_j)}\,(W_j - m_j)$. (c) Under the joint premise, for $j \ne k$: $E[\psi_j\psi_k \mid L] = \frac{Y_jY_k(W_j - m_j)(W_k - m_k)}{q_jq_k}\,E\left[\frac{Z_j - \gamma_j}{\gamma_j(1 - \gamma_j)}\right]E\left[\frac{Z_k - \gamma_k}{\gamma_k(1 - \gamma_k)}\right] = 0$. (d) For a ratio mean $\hat m = \overline{IV}/\bar I$ of a cell with indicator $I$: $\hat m - m = \frac{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i(V_i - m)}{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i}$, exactly. (e) For $G$ standard normal and $0 < u < 1$: $\Pr(2\Phi(-|G|) \le u) = u$. (f) If $p_1, \ldots, p_5$ are independent and uniform on $(0, 1)$, then $-2\sum_{j}\log p_j$ has the $\chi^2_{10}$ distribution.
canonical_claim.note: The numbers in the corrected sentence are data results, not formal content: the validator's recalculation from the deposited data gives $T = 12.143048970510$ and $\Pr(\chi^2_{10} \ge T) = 0.275596870855$ (12.141 and 0.2757 from the rounded $p$-values printed in Table 7). The repair retains Fisher's reference distribution at the cost of a substantive new premise (asymptotic independence), which the per-list assumptions do not give (P019-T9) and which the paper's own discussion of priming and order effects does not guarantee in Study B. The joint-independence condition used here is the validator's sufficient condition for that premise; it includes the usual stable-outcome model with no cross-list spillovers, and it does not require independence between a respondent's outcomes on different lists. The validator's alternative repair replaces the Fisher clause by the covariance-aware joint Wald test ($W = 5.147$, 5 degrees of freedom, $p = 0.398$), which needs no cross-list premise but a non-singular limiting covariance.
